introduction-pipelines-are-distributed-s.core: A pipeline is a distributed system of queues, runners, caches, registries and external services. 'The build is slow' needs the same observability as production: traces, metrics and logs.

first_principles.problem: A build that went from 8 to 25 minutes is investigated by scrolling logs, and nobody knows whether it's queueing, cache misses or a slow test.
truths: Many components contribute to build time.
Logs alone don't show where time goes.
derivation: Model each **pipeline run as a trace**.
Each **job and step as a span**.
Emit **metrics** (queue time, duration, cache hit rate).

analogy.title: An airport delay announcement
analogy.story: 'Delayed' could mean a late plane, crew, weather or baggage. You need breakdowns to fix it.
analogy.breaks: Instrumentation adds a little overhead and needs maintaining.

steps.label: Effect

check.q: Why treat pipelines as distributed systems?
check.a: Many independent components (queues, runners, caches, services) contribute to their behaviour and performance.

opentelemetry-for-cicd.core: OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral way to emit traces, metrics and logs from pipelines, through CI plugins and exporters or CLI wrappers like otel-cli, which you can send to any backend (Jaeger, Honeycomb, Grafana Tempo).

first_principles.problem: Each CI vendor has its own proprietary insights, so cross-tool analysis is impossible.
truths: Spans can be created around any command.
Context propagation links steps into one trace.
derivation: Create a **root span** per pipeline run.
Wrap jobs and steps as **child spans** (otel-cli exec).

analogy.title: A universal flight-tracking format
analogy.story: Every airline reports in the same format, so one dashboard can track all of them.
analogy.breaks: CI semantic conventions are still maturing, so attribute names vary.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every run appears as a trace waterfall.

key-metrics-queue-time-vs-execution-time.core: Total build time = queue time (waiting for a runner) + setup time (checkout, caches) + execution time (actual work). Each has different fixes, so decompose before optimising.

first_principles.problem: Teams optimise tests when the real problem is jobs waiting 10 minutes for a runner.
truths: Execution time reflects the work itself and caching.
derivation: Measure **queue time** → add runners or autoscale.
Measure **setup time** → fix caches and images.
Measure **execution time** → parallelise, use TIA, speed up tests.
Track **p50 and p95**, not just averages.

analogy.title: Waiting at a restaurant
analogy.story: Time to get a table (queue), to get menus and water (setup), and cooking time (execution) all need different fixes.
analogy.breaks: Averages hide tail pain, because developers feel the p95.

check.q: If queue time dominates, what's the fix?
check.a: More runner capacity or autoscaling, not faster tests.

building-a-ci-observability-dashboard.core: A useful CI dashboard answers concrete questions: are builds getting slower (trends), where does time go (queue, setup, execution), what's flaky (failure rates per test), and how reliable is main (success rate, MTTR of red main).

first_principles.problem: Raw telemetry without curated panels doesn't drive action.
truths: Alerts need thresholds tied to impact.
derivation: Panel: **main success rate**; alert on red main beyond N minutes.

analogy.title: A car's dashboard
analogy.story: Speed, fuel and warning lights, not raw sensor dumps.
analogy.breaks: Too many panels dilute attention, so keep it focused.
